title: System Boot Process
summary: The full chain from power-on to a running shell — firmware, bootloader, kernel, init — and where boot failures typically occur.

slides.markdown:
Booting is a chain of increasingly capable programs, each one loading and handing off to the next: firmware finds a bootloader, the bootloader finds a kernel, the kernel finds an init process, and init finally starts everything you actually care about.

Each handoff is a place a boot can fail, and knowing the chain — firmware → bootloader → kernel → init — is what lets you diagnose *where* a broken boot is stuck instead of guessing at "the computer won't start."

slides.sectionTitle: The boot sequence overview: firmware to bootloader to kernel to init
slides.markdown:
Four handoffs happen in strict order. **Firmware** (BIOS/UEFI) runs first because it's the only code the CPU can find with nothing else loaded — it lives in a chip on the motherboard, not on the disk. Firmware's whole job is finding and starting a **bootloader** (GRUB, for example) stored somewhere it knows to look.

The bootloader's job is finding and loading a **kernel** image into memory and jumping to it — the kernel doesn't know how to find itself. Once running, the kernel initializes hardware and then starts **init** (PID 1), the very first user-space process, which is responsible for bringing up every other service and process on the system.

Each stage exists because the previous stage is too limited to do the next stage's job — firmware can't run a full OS, a bootloader can't manage a running kernel, and a kernel by itself has no concept of "which services should be running."

Both are firmware standards for the very first code that runs, but UEFI is the modern replacement addressing BIOS's real limitations.

| | BIOS | UEFI |
|---|---|---|
| Boot disk limit | MBR partitioning — max ~2TB disks, 4 primary partitions | GPT partitioning — much larger disks, many more partitions |
| Boot process | Runs 16-bit real-mode code, loads a boot sector | Runs its own pre-OS environment, can execute drivers and apps |
| Security | None built in | Secure Boot — cryptographically verifies the bootloader before running it |
| Boot speed | Generally slower, more legacy compatibility steps | Generally faster, more parallel initialization |

**How to decide which you're dealing with:** if a system boots from a GPT disk larger than 2TB, or has Secure Boot enabled, it's UEFI — BIOS simply can't do either.

Before firmware even looks for a bootloader, it runs **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) — a quick check that essential hardware (CPU, RAM, basic I/O) is present and functioning. This is why a machine with no RAM installed beeps or shows an error instead of silently failing to boot: POST caught the problem before anything OS-related was even attempted.

Firmware also does minimal hardware initialization here — enough to talk to storage devices and a display — but deliberately not a full driver stack; that's the kernel's job later, with real, complete drivers.

POST failures are diagnosable independent of any OS or disk: they're reported via beep codes or POST codes on many motherboards, which is a strong signal for "this is a hardware problem, not a software boot problem."

slides.sectionTitle: Bootloaders: GRUB and the boot chain
slides.markdown:
**GRUB** (GRand Unified Bootloader) is the dominant Linux bootloader, and it typically loads in two stages precisely because the space firmware hands it initially is tiny. Stage 1 is a minimal piece of code small enough to fit where the firmware looks (the MBR boot sector, or the EFI system partition on UEFI); its only job is loading the much larger, more capable Stage 2, which actually understands filesystems, can present a boot menu, and knows how to load a real kernel image plus an initial RAM disk (initrd/initramfs).

That initramfs matters: it's a small, temporary root filesystem loaded into memory alongside the kernel, containing just enough drivers and tools to mount the *real* root filesystem — necessary because the kernel might need, say, a RAID or encryption driver to even reach the real root disk, and that driver has to come from somewhere before the real filesystem is available.

This is also the layer where dual-boot menus live — GRUB's Stage 2 is what shows you a list of installed OSes and lets you pick one before handing off to that OS's kernel.

The pattern worth internalizing: at every single handoff, the previous stage's code is finished and will never run again until the next reboot — a kernel panic can't be "fixed" by the bootloader retrying, because the bootloader has already exited that role.

This is why boot failures are diagnosed by figuring out which stage you got stuck *in*, not by treating "it won't boot" as one undifferentiated problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Kernel initialization: mounting root filesystem, starting init
slides.markdown:
Once the bootloader jumps into the kernel, the kernel takes over hardware initialization for real: it sets up memory management, initializes CPU cores, and loads the actual drivers needed for the devices it finds (often far more complete than firmware's minimal initialization).

Using the initramfs from the previous slide, it mounts whatever drivers are needed to reach the real root filesystem, then performs a **pivot** or **switch root** — swapping the temporary initramfs root for the real one, at which point the initramfs's job is done and it's typically discarded.

With a real root filesystem mounted, the kernel's very last act in the boot sequence is starting **init** as process ID 1 — from this point forward, the kernel steps back into its ongoing role as resource manager, and init drives everything else that starts.

slides.sectionTitle: init systems: SysV init vs systemd
slides.markdown:
**SysV init**, the traditional Unix approach, starts services sequentially through numbered shell scripts in runlevel directories — simple and easy to read, but slow and with no built-in way to express "service B needs service A running first" beyond script ordering. **systemd**, now the default on most major Linux distributions, replaces this with declarative unit files and dependency-graph-based parallel startup.

| | SysV init | systemd |
|---|---|---|
| Startup order | Sequential, numbered scripts | Parallel, based on declared dependencies |
| Config style | Shell scripts in `/etc/rc3.d/` etc. | Declarative `.service` unit files |
| Extra features | None built in | Socket activation, cgroup resource control, `journald` logging |
| Status command | `service <name> status` | `systemctl status <name>` |

**How to decide which you're on:** `systemctl status` working tells you immediately — depth on systemd's internals continues in Linux/Unix Internals.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: confusing bootloader failure vs kernel panic vs init failure when diagnosing
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The machine won't boot, so the problem must be in the OS installation."

**Why it's wrong:** "won't boot" collapses at least three completely different failure classes with different fixes. A **bootloader failure** (missing GRUB config, corrupted boot sector) typically shows a GRUB error or drops to a rescue prompt before any kernel messages appear at all. A **kernel panic** shows extensive kernel log output first, then a clear panic message and stack trace — the kernel started but hit a fatal, unrecoverable error. An **init failure** means you see full kernel boot output, the kernel handed off successfully, but the system hangs or drops to an emergency shell during service startup — the kernel is fine, one specific service or the init system itself is broken.

**Correct model:** read *how far the boot log got* before diagnosing further — it directly tells you which of the three stages failed, and each has a completely different fix (repair the bootloader, check kernel/driver compatibility, or debug a specific systemd unit).

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: fast boot and predictable boot times at scale
slides.markdown:
In cloud and container environments, boot time itself is a first-class engineering metric, not just a convenience. A full VM boot — firmware, bootloader, kernel, init, service startup — commonly takes 10-30+ seconds; that's why autoscaling systems that need to react to a traffic spike in seconds often can't just boot a fresh VM per request.

This is exactly why containers (which skip firmware, bootloader, and kernel boot entirely — they share the host's already-running kernel and only start their own init-equivalent process and application) start in milliseconds, and why serverless platforms invest heavily in "warm pools" of pre-booted execution environments to avoid paying full boot latency on the cold path.

A staff-level answer to "why is our autoscaling slow to react" often traces back to exactly this chain: recognizing that a literal OS boot (not just application startup) is on the critical path is what unlocks the real fix — pre-warming, or switching to a lighter-weight isolation model that skips most of this chain.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
`journalctl -b` on a systemd system shows the full boot log for the current (or a previous, with `-b -1`) boot — the first tool to reach for when a server came back up in a degraded state after a reboot, since it shows exactly which services started, in what order, and which failed.

Cloud instance "boot diagnostics" features (AWS EC2 serial console output, for example) exist specifically to capture early boot output — firmware and kernel messages — that would otherwise be invisible once SSH access depends on services that haven't started yet; this is often the only way to debug a VM that boots into a state where you can't even SSH in.

When an on-call engineer says "the box came back up but service X never started after the last reboot," the fastest triage is usually the same triage learned here: check how far boot progressed, then narrow to the specific stage and unit that failed.
